items.prompt: Ben and Rosa have both guessed rain for 20 years. When Rosa says '90% confident,' it rains about 89% of the time. When Ben says '90% confident,' it rains only about 58% of the time. What does this difference actually measure?
choices: Who has read more books and articles about weather forecasting over the years
Whether a stated confidence level matches the actual hit rate across many such calls
Who is naturally more optimistic in how they talk about uncertain outcomes
Who has sharper eyesight for reading cloud patterns correctly each morning
items.explanation: Calibration measures the match between a stated confidence number and the real hit rate for calls made at that confidence level — not general knowledge, personality, or any one-off guess. Rosa's numbers track reality closely; Ben's don't, even with identical experience.
items.reference:
The claim: Calibration is about whether your stated confidence matches your actual hit rate — not about how many facts you know.

Why: Ben and Rosa both guessed rain for 20 years. Rosa's '90% confident' calls are right ~89% of the time; Ben's are right only ~58% of the time — same experience, different calibration.

Across many predictions at a given stated confidence, their actual hit rate matches that stated number
They never state a confidence level below 90 percent on any prediction they make
They always double-check their reasoning carefully before committing to a final answer
items.explanation: Well-calibrated is specifically about the match between a stated confidence level and the actual hit rate at that level, checked across many predictions — not about raw accuracy or caution.
items.reference:
The claim: Calibration is about whether your stated confidence matches your actual hit rate — not about how many facts you know.

Why: Ben and Rosa both guessed rain for 20 years. Rosa's '90% confident' calls are right ~89% of the time; Ben's are right only ~58% of the time — same experience, different calibration.

items.reference:
The claim: Overconfidence means your stated confidence is higher than your real hit rate.

Why: Ben says '90% confident' but is only right ~58% of the time — the stated number overstates how sure he should actually be.

items.reference:
